newsitem.title: KYRGYZSTAN: Iran says coalition rule is key to Afghan peace.
newsitem.headline: Iran says coalition rule is key to Afghan peace.

text.p: Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said on Wednesday the creation of a broad coalition government was essential for peace in Afghanistan and he urged unspecified foreign powers to stay out of the conflict.

"We believe that all warring groups in Afghanistan should resolve all their problems by peaceful means...We think that Afghanistan should not be ruled by a single group," Velayati told a news conference in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, at the end of a two-day visit to the former Soviet republic.
Last month Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban militia, in control of most of the country since last year, launched a large-scale offensive in the north against opposition forces.
The Taleban are currently fighting troops of opposition guerrilla commander Ahmad Shah Masood to regain control over strategic points it seized and then lost in fierce battles.

Velayati, whose country is also ruled according to Islamic law but has repeatedly criticised the Taleban for its extremist interpretations of Islam, said Tehran believed the Taleban's success was due to the support of other states in the region.

"Those foreign states which interfere into Afghanistan's internal affairs should stop their actions because this involvement kindles the flame of war and thwarts the establishment of peace in this country," he said.

Velayati declined to name the countries backing the Taleban. Afghanistan's opposition has said Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, which have recognised the Taleban government in Kabul, are supporting the militia.

Russia and the five former Soviet Central Asian states of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan have voiced fears that regional stability could be shattered by the advent of militant Taleban-style Islam.
They also fear an influx of refugees if the Taleban conquer northern Afghanistan. Iran also borders Afghanistan and Velayati echoed these fears.
"We are concerned about the situation in Afghanistan, because Central Asian states are our neighbours and must live in conditions of security," he said.
"In the nearest future we will need a common conference of the neighbouring states to seek a solution to the conflict."
